Publisher XML converted to located text (jats_text): abstract and figure/table captions only

entry.evidence: The fundamental question addressed by this study is: to what degree detailed fault architectures and gas seeps can be detected and resolved in seismic data?

sequences.source_document: Faleide et al. 2022, published PDF and XML text

steps.action: Pose the question of how far detailed fault architecture and gas seeps can be detected and resolved in seismic data, framed by CO2 storage monitoring.
steps.quote: to what degree detailed fault architectures and gas seeps can be detected and resolved in seismic data?

steps.action: Assemble existing high-resolution P-Cable and conventional 3D seismic volumes over fault F2 in the Hoop area, plus logs from well 7325/4-1, and characterize their frequency and resolution.
steps.quote: The dominant frequency is 150 Hz (P-Cable) and 40 Hz (conventional), corresponding to a vertical seismic resolution of about 5 m and 20 m

steps.action: Take the baseline fault and horizon interpretation (scenario 2.4) from the authors' earlier study and depth-convert it into the 32-layer baseline model M1.
steps.quote: The baseline model (Fig. 3) is adopted from Faleide et al. (2021)

steps.action: Classify the layers into four lithologies by placing sand and shale lines on the gamma-ray log, supported by PEF and density/neutron logs.
steps.quote: therefore all layers with GR < 75 is defined as sandstone in this study

steps.action: Apply the outcrop-derived throw versus damage-zone-width scaling laws of Schueller et al. (2013) to all lithologies to size the inner and outer damage zones along F2.
steps.quote: have been utilized to make a damage zone for the F2 fault

steps.action: Design five alternative fault-architecture scenarios (M2-M6): a damage zone, CO2 in hanging-wall and/or footwall fractures, an isolated 5 m fracture corridor, and CO2 leaking from a reservoir.
steps.quote: In two models (M5 and M6), one isolated fracture corridor caused by fold-crest dilation or fault-tip process zone

steps.action: Assign Vp, Vs and density to each layer from well logs and Gardner's rule, then perturb them in the damage zones, fracture corridor and CO2-filled fractures using literature percentages (Botter; Sigernes; Agofack et al. 2018).
steps.quote: deformation bands in sandstones cause a 30% increase in Vp and Vs for the inner damage zone and 15% for the outer damage zone

steps.action: Compute Zoeppritz reflectivity and convolve it with simplified, parameter-designed 2D point-spread functions to produce PSDM-like synthetic sections, with PSF-filtered coloured noise added.
steps.quote: a simplified and idealized version of the PSF-based convolution modelling is used by directly designing PSFs from a few key parameters

steps.action: Amplitude-calibrate all synthetics against a single unit horizontal reflector test so that input reflectivity and seismic amplitudes are directly comparable.
steps.quote: an input – single – horizontal reflector of strength +1 yields a flat reflection with a peak of amplitude +1

steps.action: Fix standard parameters (45° illumination, 0° incidence, 90 Hz P-Cable wavelet) for all models, plan wavelet/incidence and illumination variants for M2 and M5, and choose difference plots and wiggle traces as comparison tools.
steps.quote: Two of the models, M2 and M5, are tested with both wavelets and different incident angles

steps.action: Compare each synthetic section (M1-M6) with its geological input model, noting which fault tips, segments, damage zones, the fracture corridor and the CO2 zones are imaged.
steps.quote: the upper fault tip of F2b cannot be identified, thereby deviating from the geological model

steps.action: Compare the models with one another and against baseline M1 through difference plots and superposed wiggle traces, isolating the effect of damage zones and of CO2.
steps.quote: the difference plots and the superposed seismic wiggle traces for the comparisons between two and two models document differences

steps.action: Rerun M2 and M5 with the conventional wavelet and a 20° incident angle; the fault block is unresolved but the damage zone and fracture corridor remain detectable.
steps.quote: there is more interference of the reflections in the conventional synthetic section

steps.action: Vary the illumination angle for M2 (30°, 45°, 90°); imaging is good at 45° and above and poor at 30°.
steps.quote: has problems imaging most of the fault segments

steps.action: Compare damage-zone widths suggested by the variance cube with outcrop-based global trend lines and with Alaei and Torabi (2017).
steps.quote: yield conceivable damage zones that are wider than those predicted by outcrop-based global trend lines

steps.action: Compare the synthetic fracture-corridor signature with unexplained throw-free dipping features in real conventional seismic from the Fingerdjupet Subbasin and the Hoop Graben, and interpret those features as joint zones.
steps.quote: they appear strikingly similar to fracture corridors encountered in the synthetic seismic sections, suggesting they represent tabular zones of joints

steps.action: Keep the findings: damage zones strengthen and widen fault signals, high-resolution data can outline damage zones and a 5 m fracture corridor, CO2-filled fractures are detectable, and illumination of 45° or more is needed.
steps.quote: CO2-filled fractures in the damage zone and in the fracture corridor give a stronger seismic response than models without CO2

tree.answer: Seismic expression of fault damage zones, fracture corridors and gas seeps
No; the structures are sub-seismic, so they are imaged through synthetic forward modelling
Characterize detection and resolution thresholds of seismic imaging
No rival hypotheses; six geological scenarios (M1-M6) serve as alternatives
Yes; the scenarios give distinguishable synthetic signatures in difference plots
Conditions set in silico (model content, wavelet, incident angle, illumination)
Partly; features survive the conventional wavelet with reduced resolution, and imaging fails at 30° illumination
Kept: the features are detectable in high-resolution synthetics under illumination of 45° or more

end.claim: In 2D PSF-based synthetic seismic, fault damage zones, a fracture corridor 5 m at its widest and CO2-filled fractures are detectable (resolved in high-resolution, mostly only detected in conventional data) when illumination is 45° or more, the average dip of the main fault.

decisive_move.sentence: The PSF-based convolution modelling of the conditioned fault scenarios produces the synthetic images on which every detectability statement rests.

gates.evidence: The seismic and well data pre-existed and no hypothesis directed their acquisition. Detectability is judged visually against the known input models and the M1 baseline; a feature could have failed to appear (e.g. the F2b tip in M1, imaging at 30° illumination), but no detection criterion or threshold was fixed in advance. The standard parameters in Table 3 were set before the results, but this is design, not registration.

imports.item: Point-spread function used to emulate PSDM resolution and illumination
Fourier transform of the PSDM filter to obtain the PSF, and convolution with reflectivity

novelty_claims.quote: The Hoop area was selected because of its unique database for such a [...]
has the potential to narrow the gap between seismic and outcrop data
provide a unique opportunity to investigate the use of high-resolution P-Cable data

limits: The XML text contains only the abstract and captions, so body steps are cited by printed page. All results are synthetic and 2D. The damage-zone elastic perturbations and CO2 effects are literature-based conceptual percentages, not measured here, and their effect on the result is not varied: only the geophysical parameters are tested. Detection is judged visually from figures; no quantitative detection threshold or signal-to-noise level is reported, although noise scaling is mentioned. The M2-M6 synthetics are not compared with the real P-Cable image of F2, so the paper does not show whether the real fault resembles M1 or the damage-zone models (inference). No review file was supplied, although the acknowledgements name Charlotte Botter and two anonymous reviewers. Sub-claims at other statuses: the interpretation of real Fingerdjupet and Hoop Graben features as fracture corridors is a suggestive best_explanation with no rivals tested beyond minor faults; the inference that damage zones are wider than outcrop trends is a qualitative comparison; the CO2 monitoring guidance is an untested implication. Composition none_fits because the walk is a scenario forward-modelling study (question, conditioned scenarios, simulation, comparison, sensitivity tests) without rival exclusion, trace series, or capability-first sequence.

disagreements.target: outcrop-based global trend lines for damage-zone width
disagreements.support: Variance-cube discontinuities 60-80 m wide, read together with Alaei and Torabi (2017), suggest subsurface damage zones wider than outcrop scaling predicts.
disagreements.quote: yield conceivable damage zones that are wider than those predicted by outcrop-based global trend lines

disagreements.target: routine interpretation of throw-free dipping features in conventional seismic (Fingerdjupet Subbasin, Hoop Graben)
disagreements.support: The synthetic fracture-corridor signature resembles these features, which interpreters overlook or cannot explain, suggesting they are joint zones rather than minor faults.
disagreements.quote: these features are overlooked as no obvious explanation is available; they are not minor faults as they lack evidence [...]

disagreements.target: common practice of displaying seismic sections with high vertical exaggeration
disagreements.support: The authors argue that vertical exaggeration masks lateral resolution problems and display most of their sections at 1:1 scale.
disagreements.quote: Seismic sections are indeed often displayed with a high vertical exaggeration, which actually masks the impact of lateral resolution issues

alternatives_considered.reason: simplification; follows Torabi et al. (2020), who find similar trends irrespective of lithology

alternatives_considered.chosen: inner (W10) and outer (W1-W10) damage zones only
alternatives_considered.reason: W5 zone appears narrow in field observations

alternatives_considered.alternatives: PSFs from detailed survey information and a velocity model
alternatives_considered.reason: lack of detailed survey information and a velocity model

alternatives_considered.chosen: model combining seismic and well data with outcrop-derived empirical laws
alternatives_considered.alternatives: outcrop-conditioned models; analogue models; numerical discrete element models
alternatives_considered.reason: outcrops rely on single locations and often lack measured petrophysical parameters

alternatives_considered.reason: gas expected above c. 800 m depth along a shallow fault
